subject: physical-education
unitTitle: Lifetime Activity Audit and Adult Transition Planning
essentialQuestion: Which of the things I do now will still be possible next year?

prompts.prompt: Explain the critical features or key principle of auditing current activities against post-graduation reality in your own words.
Demonstrate or fully describe time, money, transport, facility, and social access after high school using a version your body and setting allow. A described or adapted version earns full credit.
Apply what disappears when school activity structures end in a new situation and explain the decision or adjustment you made.
Analyze a plausible technique fault, tactical error, or unsafe choice involving activities that require nothing but space and time; correct it and explain why.
Connect building a minimum viable activity week with setting a realistic first-year activity commitment and explain how one affects the other.

Present the strongest evidence from the unit task: Audit every activity the learner currently does against post-graduation constraints, then design a minimum viable activity week that would survive the worst plausible version of next year.
Identify one thing you can now do or direct yourself, one adjustment that improved it, and one next goal you set for yourself.

adaptationChoices: The audit may be written, tabled, or spoken. A learner whose next year is uncertain builds the plan against two or three scenarios instead of one.
accommodationNote: Access supports may change format, pacing, intensity, range, equipment, setting, or response mode without changing the standard being assessed. An adapted or described performance is full credit, not partial credit.
neverRequires: This task never requires body weight, height, BMI, or body-fat percentage.
This task never requires calorie counting or a diet or weight-loss goal.
This task never requires disclosing private medical history, a diagnosis, or sexual history.
This task never requires a photograph, video, or voice recording of the learner as proof.
This task never requires a public performance or an audience.
